events.description: Kidnapping of WSJ reporter Daniel Pearl, allegedly planned and carried out by Omar Saeed Sheikh; Pearl was then beheaded by KSM.
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed captured in Rawalpindi.
Pakistani court overturns Omar Saeed Sheikh's convictions; he remains in custody pending a higher court review.
Pakistan bans FDD's Long War Journal (spring/early summer 2012 per Roggio), confirmed via a contact in Pakistan's information ministry.
After 9/11, Powell and Armitage present seven demands to Pakistan; Musharraf reportedly agrees.
Al-Qaeda fighters flee the Tora Bora mountains; Pakistan helped capture some of them.
At the start of the US invasion, Sufi Muhammad sent over 10,000 fighters from Pakistan to fight alongside the Taliban.
Atiyah Abd al-Rahman's mid-2010 assessment that al-Qaeda operated at a 'medium tempo' during the peak of the drone campaign.
Taliban announce the death of Jalaluddin Haqqani; al-Qaeda leadership and Taliban eulogize him.
Lashkar-e-Taiba raid on Mumbai with ISI backing, per the hosts. Roggio says 'December 2007'; the actual attack was in November 2008.
Lashkar-e-Taiba attack on Mumbai, which hosts say was directed by ISI members who gave orders to the attackers. Hosts state December 2007, but the real attack was in Nov 2008.
Conflicting reports that Hakimullah Mehsud had been killed, which turned out to be false.
Faisal Shahzad attempted to detonate a car bomb in Times Square; the TTP posted a video claiming it with Hakimullah Mehsud.
Pakistani military raid on the Red Mosque (Lal Masjid) in Islamabad. One of its two founders was captured and some people were killed. This led to the formation of the TTP.
Formation of the TTP after the Red Mosque raid, followed by its takeover of the tribal areas.
TTP seized control of Buner after several failed peace deals; the Pakistani military then retook it.

Gen. Tariq Khan invited Bill Roggio on a tour of South Waziristan. Khan's Peshawar hotel headquarters was then hit by a suicide attack (hosts say about 50 killed), and Khan told Roggio it was not a good time to come.
Roggio spoke at the Marshall Center in Germany; Pakistani officers could not name a single Haqqani commander killed by the Pakistani military.
actors: George C. Marshall European Center for Security Studies

events.description: Roggio testified before Congress, saying Pakistan supports the Haqqani Network and the Taliban and that Zawahiri pledged allegiance to the new Taliban leader.
The Trump administration adopted a get-tough policy on Pakistani safe havens under McMaster, then lost interest.
US-Taliban withdrawal deal negotiated in Doha by Khalilzad; the hosts note it says nothing about Pakistan.

key_claims: The Pakistani military and intelligence establishment has sheltered the Haqqani Network since the 1980s, and Taliban leaders have directed the Afghan insurgency from Pakistani soil such as Quetta.
Sirajuddin Haqqani, like his father Jalaluddin, is closely allied with al-Qaeda, as shown by files recovered in bin Laden's compound.
Pakistan did not fully comply with the seven post-9/11 US demands; the hosts grade it a mixed bag at best and give an F on the cross-border recruit and fuel demands.

Pakistan distinguishes 'good' Taliban (Afghan Taliban, Lashkar-e-Taiba, Jaish-e-Mohammed, Harkat-ul-Mujahideen, Hizbul Mujahideen) from 'bad' ones (TTP) based on whether they attack the Pakistani state; the hosts call this a distinction without a difference.
Pakistani-sponsored jihadist groups overlap with and support al-Qaeda, so the US could not defeat al-Qaeda without dismantling them; Pakistan protects its 'pet terror groups'.
Hosts believe elements of the Pakistani state knew bin Laden was in Abbottabad and that the State Department's 'end all logistical support for bin Laden' demand implied Pakistani logistical support.
Hafiz Saeed is jailed intermittently to placate the West (e.g. to avoid FATF grey-listing) and then freed by courts, which shows Pakistani non-cooperation.
The Long War Journal was banned in Pakistan in 2012 because its reporting on the state's support for jihadists threatened the Pakistani narrative, while many jihadist sites remain accessible.
The Pakistani security establishment's 'good Taliban vs bad Taliban' distinction is, in the hosts' view, a distinction without a difference.
Pakistan backs groups that do not attack the state and that advance its goals in Kashmir and Afghanistan, as part of a 'strategic depth' strategy.
Pakistani 'good Taliban', including Hafiz Gul Bahadur and the Haqqanis, facilitated the TTP's takeover of the tribal areas, creating a 'wheel of jihad'.
The Haqqani Network harbors and works with the TTP, while being backed by the Pakistani state.
Bin Laden files show al-Qaeda reviewed and edited the TTP charter, which the hosts take as evidence of influence over the group and a symbiotic relationship.
